summary.text: For \(n=550172=4\cdot343\cdot401\), a finite CRT and power-period computation shows that the residue \(63945\) is missed for every \(k\le17135926\), while a separate modular construction gives eventual coverage (indeed by \(k\le82526390\)); hence \(a(n)\ge17135927\). An Eratosthenes sieve counts exactly \(550172\) primes below \(8165754\), so \(p_n\le8165753\) and \(2(p_n-1)\le16331504<17135927\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(k)=2^k-k
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the least positive integer \(m\) for which the residues \(F(1),\ldots,F(m)\) cover every residue class modulo \(n\). We disprove the proposed inequality by taking
\[
N=550172=4\cdot137543=4\cdot343\cdot401.
\]
The argument has three parts. First, we show that the residue \(63945\) is not attained modulo \(N\) by any \(F(k)\) with \(1\leq k\leq17135926\). Second, we show directly that every residue modulo \(N\) is attained by some \(F(k)\) with \(k\leq82526390\). Thus the defining set for \(a(N)\) is nonempty and
\[
a(N)\geq17135927.
\]
Third, a sieve computation gives an upper bound for the \(550172\)-nd prime:
\[
p_{550172}\leq8165753.
\]
These bounds are incompatible with the conjecture, since
\[
2(8165753-1)=16331504<17135927.
\]
We now give all three parts in detail.

1. The residue 63945 is absent up to 17135926
------------------------------------------------

Suppose first that \(k\geq2\) and that \(F(k)\equiv63945\pmod N\). Adding \(k\) gives the equivalent congruence
\[
2^k\equiv63945+k\pmod N. \tag{1}
\]
We reduce (1) modulo the three factors \(4,343,401\).

Modulo \(4\), since \(k\geq2\), we have \(2^k\equiv0\pmod4\). As \(63945\equiv1\pmod4\), (1) implies
\[
k\equiv3\pmod4. \tag{2}
\]

The following two periodicity computations are used:
\[
2^{200}\equiv1\pmod{401},\qquad 2^{147}\equiv1\pmod{343}. \tag{3}
\]
Both are straightforward modular exponentiations by repeated squaring. Consequently,
\[
2^k\equiv2^{k\bmod200}\pmod{401},
\qquad
2^k\equiv2^{k\bmod147}\pmod{343}. \tag{4}
\]

Put \(a=k\bmod200\), so \(0\leq a<200\). The congruence modulo \(401\) in (1) becomes
\[
2^a\equiv63945+k\pmod{401}. \tag{5}
\]
For each \(a\in\{0,\ldots,199\}\), define
\[
J(a)=a+200s_a,
\]
where
\[
s_a=\bigl(( (2^a\bmod401)+80014-a)\,399\bigr)\bmod401. \tag{6}
\]
Here \(63945\equiv186\pmod{401}\), \(80014\equiv-186\pmod{401}\), and
\[
200\cdot399\equiv1\pmod{401}.
\]
It follows from (6) that
\[
J(a)\equiv a\pmod{200},
\qquad
63945+J(a)\equiv2^a\pmod{401}. \tag{7}
\]
Also \(0\leq J(a)<80200=200\cdot401\). Conversely, the Chinese remainder theorem shows that (7) uniquely determines \(J(a)\) modulo \(80200\). Therefore, if (5) holds and \(a=k\bmod200\), then
\[
k\equiv J(a)\pmod{80200}. \tag{8}
\]
Thus every possible \(k\) satisfying the congruences modulo \(401\) has the form
\[
k=80200i+J(a) \tag{9}
\]
for some \(0\leq a<200\) and \(i\geq0\). If in addition \(k<17135927\), then \(i<214\), because
\[
80200\cdot214=17162800>17135927.
\]
Condition (2) further requires \(J(a)\equiv3\pmod4\).

It remains only to test the congruence modulo \(343\). The following exhaustive finite modular computation is made. For each \(a=0,1,\ldots,199\), compute \(J(a)\) from (6). Whenever \(J(a)\equiv3\pmod4\), and for every \(i=0,1,\ldots,213\) such that
\[
80200i+J(a)<17135927,
\]
compute both sides modulo \(343\). In every case one obtains
\[
2^{(80200i+J(a))\bmod147}\not\equiv
63945+80200i+J(a)\pmod{343}. \tag{10}
\]
This is a finite check involving at most \(200\cdot214\) pairs. Modular powers are reduced first by the period \(147\), so each comparison only requires an exponent between \(0\) and \(146\). The check is precisely an exhaustive test of the displayed formula (10), with no unexamined values in the stated ranges.

Now assume for contradiction that (1) holds for some \(2\leq k<17135927\). Let \(a=k\bmod200\). By the congruence modulo \(401\), (8) holds, so writing \(i=\lfloor k/80200\rfloor\) gives
\[
k=80200i+J(a),\qquad i<214.
\]
The congruence modulo \(4\) says \(J(a)\equiv k\equiv3\pmod4\). Finally, by (3) and (4), the congruence modulo \(343\) in (1) says
\[
2^{(80200i+J(a))\bmod147}\equiv
63945+80200i+J(a)\pmod{343},
\]
contradicting (10). Hence (1), and therefore \(F(k)\equiv63945\pmod N\), is impossible for every \(2\leq k<17135927\).

The remaining case is \(k=1\). Here
\[
F(1)=2^1-1=1,
\]
which is not congruent to \(63945\) modulo \(550172\). We have therefore proved
\[
F(k)\not\equiv63945\pmod{550172}
\quad\text{for every }1\leq k\leq17135926. \tag{11}
\]

2. The covering condition eventually holds
--------------------------------------------

For completeness, we directly prove that the set of covering indices is nonempty; in fact all residues are covered by \(k\leq82526390\).

We first use the following finite calculation:

For every residue \(t'\in\{0,1,\ldots,195\}\), there is an integer \(r\) with
\[
2\leq r<590,
\quad t'+r\equiv0\pmod4,
\quad 2^r\equiv t'+r\pmod{49}. \tag{12}
\]
This is checked by trying \(r=0,1,\ldots,589\) for each of the \(196\) values of \(t'\), retaining only \(r\geq2\). The conditions depend on \(t'\) only modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,49)=196\). Therefore, for every integer \(t\), not just for \(0\leq t<196\), there is an \(r\) satisfying
\[
2\leq r<590,
\quad t+r\equiv0\pmod4,
\quad 2^r\equiv t+r\pmod{49}. \tag{13}
\]

Fix any \(t\) with \(0\leq t<N\), and choose \(r\) as in (13). Write
\[
X=2^r.
\]
We shall construct \(k\) such that
\[
2^k\equiv t+k\pmod N, \tag{14}
\]
which is equivalent to \(F(k)\equiv t\pmod N\).

Set
\[
c=X+687715-(t+r), \qquad 687715=5\cdot137543. \tag{15}
\]
This is a nonnegative integer. Indeed, \(X\geq4\), \(t\leq550171\), and \(r\leq589\), so
\[
X+687715\geq687719>550760\geq t+r.
\]
Moreover, \(687715\) is divisible by \(49\), and (13) gives \(X\equiv t+r\pmod{49}\). Hence \(49\mid c\). Write
\[
c=49u. \tag{16}
\]

Now note that
\[
137543=49\cdot2807,
\]
and the modular computation
\[
600\cdot2138\equiv1\pmod{2807} \tag{17}
\]
shows that \(2138\) is the inverse of \(600\) modulo \(2807\). Define
\[
q=(2138u)\bmod2807,
\]
so \(0\leq q<2807\). Then
\[
600q\equiv u\pmod{2807}.
\]
Multiplying by \(49\) and using \(29400=49\cdot600\), we obtain
\[
29400q\equiv49u=c\pmod{137543}. \tag{18}
\]
By (15),
\[
t+r+c=X+5\cdot137543,
\]
so (18) implies
\[
t+r+29400q\equiv X\pmod{137543}. \tag{19}
\]

A further modular exponentiation gives
\[
2^{29400}\equiv1\pmod{137543}. \tag{20}
\]
Define
\[
k=r+29400q. \tag{21}
\]
Using (20),
\[
2^k=2^{r+29400q}\equiv2^r=X\pmod{137543}. \tag{22}
\]
Equations (19), (21), and (22) therefore yield
\[
2^k\equiv t+k\pmod{137543}. \tag{23}
\]

We also have the required congruence modulo \(4\). Since \(r\geq2\) and \(k\geq r\geq2\), both \(2^r=X\) and \(2^k\) are divisible by \(4\). By (13), \(t+r\equiv0\pmod4\), while \(29400q\) is divisible by \(4\). Thus
\[
t+k=t+r+29400q\equiv0\equiv2^k\pmod4. \tag{24}
\]
Because \(\gcd(4,137543)=1\), congruences (23) and (24) combine by the Chinese remainder theorem to give
\[
2^k\equiv t+k\pmod{4\cdot137543}=\pmod{550172}.
\]
This is (14).

Finally, the constructed exponent is bounded. Since \(r\leq589\) and \(q\leq2806\),
\[
k=r+29400q\leq589+29400\cdot2806=82496989<82526390. \tag{25}
\]
Thus every residue \(t\pmod N\) is represented by \(F(k)\) for some \(1\leq k\leq82526390\).

It follows that at least one covering index exists. On the other hand, (11) says that no \(m\leq17135926\) can be a covering index, since the residue \(63945\) is then missing. Therefore the least covering index satisfies
\[
a(550172)\geq17135927. \tag{26}
\]

3. Bounding the 550172-nd prime
--------------------------------

It remains to justify the prime bound used in the comparison. Let \(\pi(M)\) denote the number of primes strictly less than \(M\). We will show
\[
\pi(8165754)=550172. \tag{27}
\]
In particular, there are \(550172\) primes at most \(8165753\), and hence
\[
p_{550172}\leq8165753. \tag{28}
\]

Here is the sieve and counting principle used to establish (27). For integers \(k,b\geq1\), index the odd numbers below \(2k\) by
\[
m_i=2i+1,\qquad 0\leq i<k.
\]
Set bit \(i\) precisely when
\[
m_i\geq3\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{minFac}(m_i)\leq b, \tag{29}
\]
where \(\operatorname{minFac}(m)\) is the least prime factor of \(m\). These bits can be generated by an odd-only sieve: for each permitted odd trial factor \(p\leq b\), mark the positions corresponding to
\[
p,3p,5p,\ldots.
\]
Indeed, the odd multiple \(p(2t+1)\) has index
\[
pt+\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
Taking the bitwise union of these arithmetic progressions gives exactly (29), provided every odd prime at most \(b\) is among the trial factors. Extra composite trial factors do no harm: a number marked by one of them still has a prime factor at most \(b\).

Suppose now that
\[
2k\leq(b+1)^2. \tag{30}
\]
Every composite odd \(m<2k\) then has least prime factor at most \(b\): otherwise its least prime factor would be at least \(b+1\), and the standard inequality \(\operatorname{minFac}(m)^2\leq m\) for composite \(m\) would contradict (30). A prime odd \(m\) is marked exactly when \(m\leq b\). Consequently, if \(C\) is the number of set bits, then counting separately the odd composites below \(2k\), the odd primes below \(2k\), the prime \(2\), and the exceptional odd number \(1\), gives the identity
\[
\pi(2k)+C+1=k+\pi(b+1). \tag{31}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\pi(2k)=k+\pi(b+1)-C-1. \tag{32}
\]

The required bit counts are obtained by a population count of the sieve bitsets. One may perform this by repeatedly pairing adjacent binary fields: initially every field is one bit; at each stage, masking the lower half of each pair and adding it to the masked, right-shifted upper half replaces every pair by the sum of its bits. After \(23\) stages this gives the number of set bits in any bitset of length at most \(2^{23}\). This procedure is simply binary addition in disjoint fields, so no carries cross a field boundary; induction over the stages proves that the final integer is the sum of all original bits.

The finite sieve computations are as follows.

* Direct enumeration gives \(\pi(8)=4\), the primes being \(2,3,5,7\).

* For \(k=27\), \(b=7\), the odd-only sieve has population count
\[
C=14.
\]
Since \(54\leq8^2\), (32) gives
\[
\pi(54)=27+\pi(8)-14-1=27+4-15=16. \tag{33}
\]

* For \(k=1429\), \(b=53\), the sieve has population count
\[
C=1029.
\]
Since \(2858\leq54^2\), equation (32), together with (33), gives
\[
\pi(2858)=1429+\pi(54)-1029-1
=1429+16-1030=415. \tag{34}
\]

* For the final sieve, take
\[
K=4082877,
\qquad B=2857.
\]
Thus
\[
2K=8165754\leq2858^2=(B+1)^2.
\]
The trial-factor filter retains odd \(p\leq53\), and for \(54\leq p\leq2857\) retains \(p\) when the preceding \(b=53\) sieve does not mark \(p\). Every odd prime \(p\leq2857\) is therefore retained: if \(p\leq53\) this is immediate, while if \(p>53\), its least prime factor is \(p>53\), so it was not marked by the small sieve. Thus the resulting large sieve still satisfies the exact characterization (29). Its population count is
\[
C=3533119. \tag{35}
\]
This is a finite odd-only sieve on \(4082877<2^{23}\) bits, followed by the field-pairing population count just described. The smaller counts \(14\) and \(1029\), and the large count (35), are obtained by explicitly forming the indicated unions of odd-multiple progressions and counting the resulting set bits.

Applying (32), then using (34), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi(8165754)
&=4082877+\pi(2858)-3533119-1\\
&=4082877+415-3533119-1\\
&=550172.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (27) and hence (28).

4. Contradiction to the conjectured inequality
-----------------------------------------------

For \(n=N=550172\), (26) gives
\[
a(N)\geq17135927.
\]
By (28),
\[
2(p_N-1)\leq2(8165753-1)=16331504.
\]
Since
\[
17135927>16331504,
\]
we conclude that
\[
a(550172)>2(p_{550172}-1).
\]
In particular, the asserted strict inequality \(a(n)<2(p_n-1)\) fails at \(n=550172\). This disproves the conjecture.
